On the same \jtNcells{} joint cells and the fixed truth changes used to develop the estimator, an exact binned iterative unfolding with the same simulation and five iterations leaves about the same median residual as the boosted-tree estimator.
Of the 144 cell-and-truth-change residuals above \SI{2}{\percent} whose diagnosis is stable under the truth resolution, pooled over five truth changes, the tree approximation dominates only 15.

Most of the 144 (121) lie in quantities that the binned response constrains weakly at the analysis exposure, with Cram\'er--Rao widths above \SI{10}{\percent}, so the regularization trades a large variance for the bias.
Longer noise-free exact iteration removes much of the residual for the GiBUU-to-GENIE change, but not for every change.
The diagnostic is binned, signal-only and noise-free, with the detector response fixed at the simulation's.
It covers only the residuals whose diagnosis is stable under the truth resolution (\SI{38}{\percent} of the joint-cell residuals above \SI{2}{\percent}).
What unbinned information could recover, the coverage failure, and the validity of any interval lie outside its scope.

Within that scope, the residual is consistent with the regularization of the inverse problem at this binning and prior, rather than with the tree approximation of the classifiers (\nsec{sec:val-departure}).

The block supersedes two earlier statistical bands, whose coverage studies are described in \nsec{sec:coverage}.
Replacing it by the charged-pion mass would change no true-$\Eavail$ bin by more than \SI{1.05}{\percent}.
Two properties must be distinguished.
The coverage of unfolded intervals is the rate at which they contain the true cross section.
The calibration of a test is the rate at which it rejects a true hypothesis.
Calibration can be obtained without validated intervals by simulating the whole analysis chain at the hypothesis, so that the estimator's bias enters the simulated null distribution.
A calibration obtained in this way is valid to the extent that the simulated chain reproduces the analysis of the data.
For GiBUU, whose sample lacks high-energy neutrinos, the domain is the \jtNcellsGiBUU{} supported cells with $\pPar<\SI{6}{GeV/c}$.
The NuWro and GiBUU comparisons contain a target difference of this kind, which the tests of Sec.~\ref{sec:joint} do not correct.

The generator tests are conditional tests of simulated hybrid null hypotheses, under which the cross section equals a prediction on every cell of a fine five-observable grid, with the MINERvA Tune~v1 composition below that grid, as defined in Sec.~\ref{sec:hypotheses}.
They are calibrated within the implemented simulation model, whose detector model has no calorimetric recoil-response uncertainty.
Under the assumptions of Sec.~\ref{sec:calibration}, their decision rule controls the familywise error rate of the ten decisions at 5\%, on average over the nuisance priors.
The rejections are not physical exclusions of the generators and provide no measurement uncertainty.

The three- and four-observable central values, the sixteen-cell five-observable result (Sec.~\ref{sec:result16}) and the joint tests use the joint-test estimator, a deterministic LightGBM with the same background treatment and refinement capacity, which removes most of the bias of purity-based subtraction at nominal truth in the highest-$W$ cells (Sec.~\ref{sec:validation}).
It motivates the different route to inference of Sec.~\ref{sec:joint}: after a descriptive comparison of the central values, the generator predictions are tested as hypotheses.

The truths are the simulation's prior; the five hybrid truths of the generator tests of Sec.~\ref{sec:joint}, each a prediction on the fine grid; NuWro shape changes in $\Eavail$ and in $(\pT,\pPar,\Eavail)$; a GENIE + MEC shape change in $(\Eavail,W)$; a GiBUU-to-GENIE $\Eavail$ ratio; a noise-free closure at the NuWro shape; and a synthetic tilt of the $q_3$ distribution at fixed $(\Eavail,W)$.
The third is the upward displacement of the external nulls by the estimator's pull toward its prior, which the calibration of Sec.~\ref{sec:joint-results} reproduces.
The calibrated tests illustrate inference with a biased estimator: the decision rule controls the familywise error rate at 5\% provided the calibration is exact.
The generator tests reject hybrid nulls, conditionally on the simulation's hadronic response.
The rejections carry over to the generator predictions themselves only under a bound on the residual below the fine grid, which has not been shown (Sec.~\ref{sec:conditions}).
Their calibration is valid to the extent that the simulated chain reproduces the analysis of the data (Sec.~\ref{sec:calibration}).
As an application, Sec.~\ref{sec:joint} tests generator predictions that the published muon-kinematic measurement already disfavours~\cite{MINERvA:2021owq}.
Every study uses the analysis simulation's detector response, except the calibration of the tests, which also draws the detector bands.
When intervals cannot be validated, tests can still be calibrated by simulating the analysis chain at the hypothesis, as in Sec.~\ref{sec:joint}.

\section{Simulation-calibrated tests of generator predictions} \label{sec:joint} Unfolded results can be compared with any prediction at truth level without simulating each generator through the detector, which is what makes the two-dimensional result reusable and the higher-dimensional central values usable for qualitative comparison, and the sixteen-cell result usable for the comparison of Sec.~\ref{sec:gen16}.
For hypothesis tests the advantage is smaller.
A test at reconstruction level would avoid the regularization bias, but it would still need the same response model.

Each external prediction would have to be folded through the analysis simulation's response, which is the hybrid construction of Sec.~\ref{sec:hypotheses}, with the same composition below the fine grid.
The tests of this section instead calibrate the unfolded statistic in simulation, so that the bias enters the null distribution rather than the decision.
We have not compared their power with that of a reconstruction-level test.

\subsection{Hypotheses and calibration} \label{sec:hypotheses} For each of five predictions $G$ (the MINERvA Tune~v1, GENIE CV, GENIE + MEC, NuWro~21.09, and GiBUU~2019), the null hypothesis $H_{0}(G)$ is that the true cross section equals $G$ on every cell of the fine grid of Sec.~\ref{sec:data}.

Below that grid, the null truth has the MINERvA Tune~v1 simulation's event composition, varied in each pseudo-experiment by the drawn interaction-model universes with every fine-cell integral held fixed.
The background is the Tune~v1 simulation's, with its uncertainty bands.
We call this hypothesis the hybrid null: it is the hypothesis the calibration simulates.
Each prediction is tested in total and in shape on the supported coarse cells of Sec.~\ref{sec:data}.
Three properties are distinct.
The hybrid null is defined exactly on the finite grid and needs no convergence.
Whether it represents the physical generator prediction depends on the composition below the fine grid and on convergence of that grid (condition~(i) below).
Calibration fidelity is whether the calibration reproduces the analysis of the data (conditions~(ii)--(iv)).
Each calibration pseudo-experiment splits the simulation at random into two halves.
The source half is reweighted per fine cell to $G$ and carries the flux, interaction-model, and detector nuisance draws.
The interaction-model bands are renormalized within each fine truth cell on the signal, so that they move only the composition within the cell, and with it the efficiency and the migrations.
The lateral detector bands enter as $\sum_{b}z_{b}\Delta_{b}$, with $\Delta_{b}$ from endpoint unfoldings of the data.
Poisson pseudo-data are drawn from the source half, and the background pseudo-data are a Poisson draw from one half of a separate background sample.
The joint-test estimator unfolds the pseudo-data with the other half of the simulation.
A \SI{1.4}{\percent} normalization, the data's rounding noise, and the prediction's finite-sample residual are then added.
The data are unfolded once, with the full simulation.

Because the $\Delta_{b}$ come from the observed data, the null distributions are conditional on these data-derived inputs, and this conditioning has not been validated (\nsec{sec:joint5d-calibration}).
A total statistic $T_{\mathrm{tot}}=r^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}r$ is formed from the residual $r=F-\mu_{G}$ of the unfolded cell values $F$ and the prediction $\mu_{G}$.
It tests the rate and the shape together, and we call it the total (rate-and-shape) test.
A shape statistic $T_{\mathrm{sh}}$ of the same form uses the normalized cell fractions, with one cell dropped.
The metric $\Sigma=V+\mathrm{diag}\,\mathrm{Var}(\mu_{G})$ adds the prediction's own finite-sample variance to $V$.

Here $V$ is a Ledoit--Wolf-shrunk covariance~\cite{LedoitWolf:2004} of \jtVn{} pilot pseudo-experiments at the Tune~v1 null, whose shrinkage floors about 80 of the 109 nearly degenerate correlation directions.
The metric influences each test's power; the null calibration determines its size.

\subsection{Decision rule and familywise error} \label{sec:calibration} The Monte Carlo $p$ value of a test is $(k+1)/(B+1)$, where $k$ of $B$ null pseudo-experiments reach the observed statistic; it is never zero.

Each decision uses the largest $p$ value over a set of shifted nulls, which add a fixed vector to every null draw: zero, half, or all of an upper bound $D$ on the simulation-size difference along the null's bias direction (condition~(iv) below), or $\pm\jtMoneKappa\,\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$, where $\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$ is the change of the noise-free unfolded result in the last step of a refinement of the null truth's grid (condition~(i)).
The ten tests are controlled at a familywise level $\alpha=\jtAlpha$ by the Holm procedure~\cite{Holm:1979}, with pseudo-experiments drawn sequentially, to at most \jtBcap{} per null.
A hypothesis is rejected only when the upper end of the two-sided 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval~\cite{Clopper:1934} of its exceedance fraction lies below its Holm threshold.

This rule rests on two assumptions: each true null's calibrated tail probability is uniformly distributed or conservative (A1), and the pseudo-experiments' exceedances are independent given the data (A2).

Under them, the probability of meeting the criterion at any number of pseudo-experiments up to \jtBcap{} is below the threshold, whatever rule determines when sampling stops, so the decision rule controls the familywise error rate of the ten decisions at 5\% (\napp{sec:joint5d-fwer}).
The calibrated size is averaged over the nuisance priors: at a fixed true value of the nuisance parameters it can exceed $\alpha$.
The error control applies to the decisions, not separately to the point estimates $(k+1)/(B+1)$.
The calibration is valid for the simulated null to the extent that the pseudo-experiment chain reproduces the analysis of the data (A1).
Every pseudo-experiment resamples the same simulated events, so measuring a rejection rate for null pseudo-data processed like the data would require an independent simulation sample.
No such rate has been measured.
The test design was fixed before any observed statistic was computed, after descriptive per-cell residuals of the data had been seen.
The computing budget of the calibration was extended by a bounded amount after the observed $p$ values were visible.
Under A1 and A2, the error control holds for any rule that decides when sampling stops, so the extension does not affect it.
Of the submitted pseudo-experiments, \jtLostCal{} for calibration and \jtLostPow{} for power did not complete within the computing time limits, and the decisions use the completed ones.
When rerun, none of the lost calibration pseudo-experiments reaches the observed statistic in any test or shifted null, so their outcomes change no decision.
A2 also requires that the pseudo-experiments were lost independently of their outcomes, which has not been shown.
Independently written code reproduces every $p$ value and decision.
The design and the rerun are described in Ref.~\cite{AnalysisNote2026}, Secs.~\ref*{N-sec:joint5d-frozen} and~\ref*{N-sec:joint5d-lost}.
\subsection{Conditions} \label{sec:conditions} The decisions rest on six conditions on the nuisance model, numbered as in \nsec{sec:joint5d-conditions}.
\emph{(i) Convergence below the fine grid.} Within each fine-grid cell the null truth has the Tune~v1 composition of the hypothesis definition.
In the $L_{2}$ norm of the per-cell relative changes, the last refinement step is \jtMoneMin--\jtMoneMax{} of the whole change from the coarse test grid.
Convergence of the fine grid has therefore not been shown, and the residual below it is unmeasured and potentially material.
The shifts $\pm\jtMoneKappa\,\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$ were set by assuming that the refinement steps shrink geometrically.
The measured $L_{2}$ ratios also allow slower convergence.

The rejections carry over from the simulated hybrid nulls to the generator predictions themselves only if replacing the Tune~v1's shape below the fine grid by $G$'s moves the noise-free unfolded result by no more than $\pm\jtMoneKappa\,\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$ along $\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$.
Showing this would require a demonstrated bound on the residual below the fine grid.
\emph{(ii) Detector and hadronic response.}\label{sec:response} The detector model is the simulation's, varied only by the drawn detector bands and a linear surrogate for the lateral bands.
It has no band for the calorimetric hadronic-energy response.

In MINERvA's recoil-energy analyses, the uncertainty of that response is derived from test-beam calorimetry~\cite{MINERvA:2015testbeam} and rises to \SI{10}{\percent} at the highest three-momentum transfers of the low-recoil measurement~\cite{MINERvA:2022incl}.
The omission matters for the rejections.

A check made after the decisions shows that the calibrated tests restricted to the matched $(\pT,\pPar)$ projection of Sec.~\ref{sec:joint-results} do not reject GENIE~2.12.10 CV ($p=\woneGcvPtTot$ in total and $\woneGcvPtShape$ in shape), so the information that rejects it involves the hadronic axes, on which a response band would act.
The net effect of the missing band on each $p$ value has not been measured.
The rejections remain conditional on the simulation's hadronic response, and their physical interpretation would require a response band drawn through the calibration.

In an exploratory sensitivity study, the simulation's reconstructed recoil energy is scaled by $\pm\SI{4}{\percent}$, the level of data--simulation agreement reported for test-beam protons, pions, and electrons of 0.35--\SI{2.0}{GeV/c}~\cite{MINERvA:2015testbeam}, and the data are re-unfolded.
In this study, every rejection stays in place against the original null distributions, and the observed statistics move by up to about \SI{11}{\percent}.
The study regenerates no null distribution and tests no other form or size of response change.
Neutrons and higher-momentum hadrons, which matter at high $W$, lie outside the test-beam sample.
The effects the study does not test are listed in \nsec{sec:joint5d-response}.
\emph{(iii) Interaction-model prior.} The prior is the analysis's \jtModelBands-band set, with negative weights of two bands clipped.
\emph{(iv) Simulation size.} The pseudo-experiments use half of the simulation and the data all of it.
The resulting shift enters as the upper-bound shift $D$.
It is at most about 0.07 null standard deviations, measured for the mean only, without noise or nuisance draws.
Repeating part of the calibration with a quarter of the simulation resolved no change of the null distributions.
Under an extrapolation to the full simulation that is conservative by design, all ten decisions remain rejected.
The two decisions closest to their boundary exceed the value at which they would change by 1.11 and 1.30 null standard deviations.
\emph{(v), (vi) Domain and prediction samples.} GiBUU lacks $E_{\nu}>\SI{20}{GeV}$, and its out-of-domain truth enters the migrations into its domain.
The predictions' own finite samples enter the metric and the simulated residuals.
\subsection{Results} \label{sec:joint-results} Table~\ref{tab:joint} shows that every test is rejected at familywise $\alpha=\jtAlpha$.
NuWro and GiBUU were generated on carbon.
Correcting both predictions to the hydrocarbon target moves both toward the data, and NuWro's total-test rejection does not survive that correction robustly.
GiBUU's deep-inelastic events on hydrogen do not conserve energy, which affects its correction and possibly its carbon prediction.
The decisions of Table~\ref{tab:joint} concern each prediction on the target it was generated for.
The target-corrected evaluations are descriptive and leave them unchanged.
As a sensitivity check outside the decision rule, a scan of the multiplier of the shift along $\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$ finds all ten rejections determined up to a multiplier of about 5.2.
The scan probes that one direction.

The calibrated null distributions differ in location: the Tune~v1 null is centred at small values, whereas the external nulls are displaced far upward by the estimator's pull toward its prior, which the calibration reproduces.

The target-corrected evaluations, the scan, and the null distributions with the observed statistics are given in Ref.~\cite{AnalysisNote2026}, Secs.~\ref*{N-sec:joint5d-ch} and~\ref*{N-sec:joint5d-results}.
